title: Trial Phases, Research Billing, Kickbacks and the Moore Case
summary: Learn what each clinical trial phase does and how large it usually is, which trial tests Medicare covers and which belong to the study budget, what makes a payment an illegal kickback, and what Moore v. Regents decided about cell lines and disclosure.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 14 Hits 7, 8 and 9 and Trap 4. Trial phases from 21 CFR 312.21 and 312.85 (eCFR, version 2026-10-01) and Burt 2016 for phase 0; trial billing from Medicare NCD 310.1 (NCD Manual chapter 1 part 4, Rev. 12590) and Breault 2020; kickbacks from 42 USC 1320a-7b and 18 USC 220 (US Code 2023 edition, govinfo); Moore v. Regents (51 Cal.3d 120, 1990) read from the opinion text on Stanford SCOCAL, with Spector-Bagdady 2021 as secondary commentary. Justia and CourtListener copies of the opinion returned 403 and were not read. The reviewer’s phase sizes (phase I 15–30, phase III 100+) differ from 21 CFR 312.21 (rv-ch14-trial-phase-sizes). The reviewer’s Moore summary omits that the ruling came at the pleading stage and that the disclosure claims were sustained against the treating physician (rv-ch14-moore-pleading-stage). The reviewer’s “kickbacks are illegal” omits the knowing-and-willful element and statutory exceptions (rv-ch14-kickback-intent-exceptions). Not taught: Number Vault rows (including the $3 billion figure, which the opinion describes as a predicted market for the cell line’s kinds of proteins), record retention, Belmont figure.

objectives: Describe the purpose and typical size of phase 0 to phase 4 clinical studies.
Distinguish routine trial costs that Medicare covers from research-only items that the study must pay for, and explain the False Claims Act risk of double billing.
State what makes a payment a kickback under federal law, name key exceptions, and summarize what Moore v. Regents held.

scenes.title: A trial comes to the lab
scenes.altText: Invented scenario: a hospital laboratory joins a drug trial. Card 1: the protocol adds an extra research panel at every visit that the patient’s doctor would never order. Card 2: an analyzer vendor offers the laboratory manager a paid resort trip if the lab switches instruments. Card 3: a physician-investigator asks a patient to sign consent for surgery while privately planning to develop and patent a cell line from the removed tissue. cues.text: Invented scenario: your hospital lab joins a drug trial, and the protocol adds a research-only panel at every visit that the patient’s own doctor would never order.
Then an analyzer vendor offers the lab manager a paid resort trip if the lab switches instruments. And a physician plans to patent a cell line from a patient’s tissue without telling the patient.
Who pays for the research panel, what is illegal about the trip, and what must the physician disclose?

scenes.title: The phase ladder
scenes.altText: Phase ladder (21 CFR 312.21 and 312.85; Burt 2016). Phase 0 card: exploratory, limited-exposure studies such as microdosing (no more than 100 µg or one-hundredth of the no-observed-adverse-effect level, whichever is lower), no therapeutic intent, not meant to test tolerability; typically one study with six to 10 participants per program. Phase 1 card: initial introduction of an investigational drug into humans; metabolism, pharmacologic actions, side effects with increasing doses; generally 20 to 80 subjects. Phase 2 card: controlled studies of effectiveness in patients with the condition plus common short-term side effects; usually no more than several hundred subjects. Phase 3 card: expanded controlled and uncontrolled trials, several hundred to several thousand subjects, to evaluate overall benefit-risk and provide an adequate basis for labeling. Phase 4 card: postmarketing studies FDA may seek at approval, such as other doses, populations or longer use.

cues.text: Phase zero studies are exploratory, with tiny exposures such as a microdose of no more than one hundred micrograms. They have no therapeutic intent and do not test tolerability; one review says a program typically needs one such study of six to ten people.

Phase one is the initial introduction of a new drug into humans: metabolism, pharmacologic actions and side effects as doses rise. Federal regulation says it generally involves twenty to eighty subjects.
Phase two runs controlled studies of effectiveness in patients who have the condition, plus common short-term side effects, usually with no more than several hundred subjects.

Phase three expands to several hundred to several thousand subjects to judge overall benefit and risk and support labeling. Phase four is postmarketing study, such as new doses, populations or longer use.

scenes.title: Who pays for trial testing
scenes.altText: Medicare clinical trial policy card (NCD 310.1): Medicare covers routine costs of qualifying clinical trials and reasonable and necessary care for complications. Routine costs include conventional care, items needed to give the investigational item, clinically appropriate monitoring, and prevention or treatment of complications. Excluded card: the investigational item itself (unless otherwise covered), items and services provided solely for data collection and analysis and not used in direct clinical management, and items the sponsor customarily provides free. Fraud card (Breault 2020): billing an insurer for what the sponsor pays is double billing; with Medicare or Medicaid it falls under the False Claims Act, and civil liability can arise even from inadequate controls without intent; nothing billable to the sponsor should be billed to participants or insurers. Safeguard token: a Medicare coverage analysis and coordination between research and billing offices before the study begins.

cues.text: Who pays? Medicare’s clinical trial policy covers routine costs of qualifying trials, such as conventional care and clinically appropriate monitoring, plus care for complications.

It excludes the investigational item itself, unless otherwise covered, items the sponsor usually provides free, and services done only for data collection and analysis that are not used to manage the patient.

Billing a patient’s insurer for something the sponsor pays is double billing. With Medicare or Medicaid it falls under the False Claims Act, and civil penalties can follow even from weak controls without intent to defraud.
The safeguard: complete a coverage analysis and coordinate research and billing offices before the study begins. So the hook’s research panel goes to the study budget, not the insurer.

props.label: Coverage analysis before the study starts

scenes.title: Kickbacks and the Moore case
scenes.altText: Anti-Kickback Statute card (42 USC 1320a-7b(b)): knowingly and willfully offering, paying, soliciting or receiving any remuneration, in cash or in kind, to induce referrals or the purchasing or ordering of items paid by a federal health care program is a felony; claims resulting from a violation are false claims. Exceptions card: properly disclosed discounts and amounts paid by an employer to a bona fide employee; EKRA (18 USC 220, 2018) applies to laboratories and any health care benefit program, and its employee exception holds only if pay does not vary by referrals, number of tests or amount billed. Moore card (Moore v. Regents, Cal. 1990): a UCLA patient with hairy-cell leukemia had his spleen removed; a cell line was developed from his cells and patented in 1984; the court rejected his conversion claim, holding the patented cell line was factually and legally distinct from the cells taken. Disclosure card: a physician seeking consent must disclose personal research or economic interests that may affect medical judgment; the complaint stated a cause of action for breach of fiduciary duty or lack of informed consent against the treating physician; this was a pleading-stage ruling, not a finding of breach.

cues.text: Kickbacks: under the federal Anti-Kickback Statute, knowingly and willfully paying or receiving anything of value, cash or in kind, to induce referrals or purchases paid by federal health programs is a felony.

There are exceptions, such as properly disclosed discounts and pay to bona fide employees. A 2018 law aimed at laboratories reaches all payers, and its employee exception fails if pay varies with referrals, test counts or amounts billed.

Moore versus Regents, California, 1990: a cell line from a leukemia patient’s cells was patented. The court rejected his property claim, calling the patented line factually and legally distinct from his cells.

But a physician seeking consent must disclose research or economic interests that may affect medical judgment. The court let fiduciary-duty and informed-consent claims against his physician proceed; it did not find a breach.

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “Research-only tests can be billed to insurance like routine care” (✓ Medicare covers routine costs; tests done only for data collection are excluded and belong to the study budget); “Phase 1 enrolls 15–30 and phase 3 just 100 or more” (✓ regulation: phase 1 generally 20–80, phase 3 several hundred to several thousand); “The Moore court found the doctors liable” (✓ it rejected conversion and let fiduciary-duty and informed-consent claims proceed at the pleading stage).

cues.text: Trap one: research-only tests can be billed to insurance like routine care. No: Medicare covers routine trial costs, while tests done only for data collection belong to the study budget.

Trap two: phase one enrolls fifteen to thirty and phase three just over one hundred. Federal regulation says phase one is generally twenty to eighty, and phase three several hundred to several thousand.
Trap three: the Moore court found the doctors liable. No: it rejected the property claim and only allowed the disclosure claims to go forward.

scenes.title: Ladder, ledger, leash
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “LADDER, LEDGER, LEASH. The phase LADDER gets wider as you climb (exploratory few, then tens, hundreds, thousands, then the market). The LEDGER has two columns: routine care to the insurer, research-only work to the study. The LEASH keeps money away from judgment: no pay tied to referrals or test volume, and disclose research or financial interests to the patient.” Tokens: ladder = phases · ledger = who pays · leash = kickbacks and disclosure. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: ladder, ledger, leash. The phase ladder widens as you climb. The ledger has two columns: routine care to the insurer, research-only work to the study. The leash keeps money away from judgment: no pay tied to referrals, and disclose your interests.

Where it breaks: phase sizes are typical ranges and phases can overlap; the ledger shown is Medicare policy, and other payers and countries differ; kickback laws need knowing and willful conduct and have exceptions; and Moore is one California decision.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “Phases widen from exploratory to postmarketing · routine trial care to the insurer, research-only tests to the study”, “No pay tied to referrals or test volume · disclose research and financial interests (Moore)”.

cues.text: Trial phases widen from tiny exploratory studies to postmarketing follow-up, insurers pay only routine trial care while research-only tests belong to the study budget, pay tied to referrals or test volume is an illegal kickback, and Moore teaches that physicians must disclose research and financial interests even though patients do not own the cell lines made from their cells.

explanation.what: Plain language: new drugs are tested in steps that start with a handful of people and grow to thousands, then continue after approval. When a patient is in a trial, their insurer pays for the normal care they would get anyway, while tests done only for the study are paid by the study. Giving or taking money or gifts to steer patients or purchases is a crime, and a doctor who stands to gain from a patient’s tissue must tell the patient. Scientific terms: investigational new drug, phase 0 (exploratory, microdose), phase 1, phase 2, phase 3, phase 4 (postmarketing), routine costs, coverage analysis, double billing, False Claims Act, Anti-Kickback Statute, remuneration, safe harbor, bona fide employee, EKRA, conversion, fiduciary duty, informed consent.
explanation.why: Phases grow in size because each step needs more evidence before more people are exposed. Payers cover clinical care, not the study’s data collection, so billing research-only tests to an insurer charges it for something it does not cover. Kickback laws exist because payments tied to referrals or orders can bend medical and purchasing decisions, and Moore applied the same idea to consent: a physician’s research or financial interest can affect judgment, so the patient must know about it.
explanation.measure: Phase 0: microdose no more than 100 µg or 1/100 of NOAEL (whichever is lower), no therapeutic intent; typically one study of 6–10 participants per program (Burt 2016). Phase 1: generally 20–80 subjects. Phase 2: usually no more than several hundred. Phase 3: several hundred to several thousand. Phase 4: postmarketing studies (21 CFR 312.21, 312.85). Medicare NCD 310.1: routine costs and complications covered; investigational item, data-collection-only items and sponsor-provided items excluded. Anti-Kickback Statute: knowing and willful remuneration for federal-program referrals or orders is a felony (42 USC 1320a-7b(b)). EKRA: laboratories, all health care benefit programs (18 USC 220). Moore v. Regents: 51 Cal.3d 120 (1990).
explanation.differs: Phase 1 (first into humans, safety and dosing, tens of subjects) vs phase 3 (expanded benefit-risk, hundreds to thousands); routine trial cost (billable) vs data-collection-only item (study budget); bona fide salary vs pay that varies with referrals or test volume; conversion (property claim, rejected in Moore) vs breach of fiduciary duty or lack of informed consent (claim allowed to proceed).
explanation.examAngle: Expect: match a phase to its purpose or size, decide whether a trial test can be billed to insurance, spot a kickback, or state what Moore held.

questions.stem: A Medicare patient enrolled in a qualifying drug trial has a research-only biomarker panel drawn at each visit solely for the study’s data analysis; the results are not used to manage the patient. Under Medicare clinical trial policy, how should the panel be handled?

options.text: Paid from research funds, not billed to Medicare
options.rationale: Correct. Medicare excludes items and services provided solely to satisfy data collection and analysis needs that are not used in direct clinical management.

options.text: Billed to Medicare as a routine trial cost
options.rationale: Incorrect. Routine costs are items generally available to beneficiaries and used in care, such as conventional care and clinically appropriate monitoring; data-collection-only tests are excluded.

options.text: Billed to both the sponsor and Medicare to cover costs
options.rationale: Incorrect. Billing both is double billing, which with Medicare falls under the False Claims Act.

options.text: Billed to Medicare because the patient signed the consent form
options.rationale: Incorrect. Consent to participate does not change what Medicare covers.

questions.stem: Under 21 CFR 312.21, which phase consists of expanded controlled and uncontrolled trials, usually of several hundred to several thousand subjects, intended to evaluate overall benefit-risk and provide an adequate basis for labeling?

options.rationale: Correct. Phase 3 studies are expanded trials of several hundred to several thousand subjects that gather the effectiveness and safety data needed for benefit-risk evaluation and labeling.
Incorrect. Phase 1 is the initial introduction into humans, focused on metabolism, pharmacologic action and dose-related side effects, generally in 20 to 80 subjects.
Incorrect. Phase 2 studies evaluate effectiveness in patients with the condition and usually involve no more than several hundred subjects.
Incorrect. Phase 4 studies are postmarketing studies conducted after approval.

questions.stem: Which statement best summarizes the California Supreme Court’s 1990 decision in Moore v. Regents of the University of California?

options.text: Moore could not sue for conversion of his cells, but his physician had to disclose research and economic interests, so the fiduciary-duty and informed-consent claims could proceed
options.rationale: Correct. The court rejected conversion, held the patented cell line legally and factually distinct from his cells, and held that a physician seeking consent must disclose personal research or economic interests.

options.text: Moore owned the patented cell line and was entitled to share in its profits
options.rationale: Incorrect. The court held that the patented cell line could not be Moore’s property.

options.text: Physicians have no duty to tell patients about research interests in their tissue
options.rationale: Incorrect. The court held that a physician must disclose personal interests, research or economic, that may affect medical judgment.

options.text: The court found the physicians liable and awarded damages for breach of fiduciary duty
options.rationale: Incorrect. The ruling addressed whether the complaint stated causes of action; it allowed the disclosure claims to proceed but made no finding of breach or award.

claims.text: Phase 1 to 4 purposes and typical sizes (21 CFR 312.21, 312.85); phase 0 exploratory microdose studies without therapeutic intent, typically six to 10 participants.
Medicare covers routine trial costs and complications but not the investigational item, data-collection-only items or sponsor-provided items.
Double billing Medicare or Medicaid falls under the False Claims Act, even without intent; coverage analysis and coordination before study start.
Anti-Kickback Statute elements, exceptions and false-claim consequence; EKRA scope and employee-pay exception.
Moore v. Regents: conversion rejected, patented cell line distinct, physician disclosure duty, fiduciary-duty and informed-consent claims stated at the pleading stage.

Reviewer figures not taught: phase 0 10–15 and phase I 15–30 subjects, phase III 100+; “lab directors should be paid by negotiated salary, not billing privileges” as a specific director rule; Moore cell-line profits over $3 billion.
claims.note: Phase figures differ from 21 CFR 312.21 and Burt 2016; the director-pay rule is taught only as the general EKRA and Anti-Kickback employee exceptions; the opinion describes $3 billion as an alleged predicted market, not realized profit.

accuracyFlags.issue: The reviewer gives phase I as 15–30 and phase III as 100+ subjects (phase 0 10–15). 21 CFR 312.21 states phase 1 is generally 20 to 80 subjects and phase 3 usually several hundred to several thousand; Burt 2016 describes phase 0 as typically one study of six to 10 participants. The lesson teaches the regulatory ranges.

The reviewer says the court “allowed claims that doctors breached fiduciary duty.” The opinion decided only that the complaint stated causes of action (a pleading-stage ruling); it overruled the treating physician’s demurrers on fiduciary-duty and informed-consent claims, sustained other defendants’ demurrers with leave to amend, and made no finding of breach. The $3 billion figure is an alleged predicted market for the cell line’s kinds of proteins, not realized profits.

The reviewer states that kickbacks (cash, travel, gifts) are illegal without qualification. The Anti-Kickback Statute requires knowing and willful conduct tied to federal health care program business and lists exceptions (properly disclosed discounts, bona fide employee pay, regulatory safe harbors); EKRA extends a similar prohibition to laboratory referrals across all payers.

The lesson describes US federal law (FDA phase definitions, Medicare NCD 310.1, Anti-Kickback Statute, EKRA) and a California court decision. Philippine trial regulation, payer rules and anti-kickback law are not covered; MTLE candidates should check local requirements.
